lessons.title: Choose employees matching a condition
rules: Return the names and salaries of employees whose salary is at least 60.
Output columns · name, salary
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: FROM selects the table, WHERE selects matching rows, and SELECT chooses output columns.

conceptExample.explanation: Select the Employee row with id 1, then return only name. The sample returns Ada.

hints: You can evaluate the salary condition from one row alone.
Try WHERE salary >= 60 after FROM Employee.
lessons.starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM Employee
-- Add a row-filtering condition here.

lessons.title: Count direct reports per manager
rules: Using only employees with managers, return the number of direct reports per manager ID as direct_reports.
Output columns · managerId, direct_reports
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: GROUP BY places rows with the same managerId in one group. Each output row now represents one manager.

conceptExample.explanation: Sum salaries of employees sharing managerId. Manager 1 has 80 + 60 + 55 + 50 + 45 = 290 in the sample. SUM adds values; COUNT(*) counts rows in the group.

hints: Rows with NULL managerId do not report to anyone.
Filter with WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL, then use GROUP BY managerId and COUNT(*).
lessons.solution:
SELECT managerId, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
FROM Employee
WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY managerId;

lessons.title: Groups with at least five direct reports
rules: Return manager IDs and counts with at least five direct reports. Exclude employees without managers.
Output columns · managerId, direct_reports
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups using aggregate results after GROUP BY.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT managerId, SUM(salary) AS team_salary
FROM Employee
WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY managerId
HAVING SUM(salary) >= 100;
conceptExample.explanation: WHERE first excludes employees with no manager ID. HAVING then keeps groups whose salary total is at least 100. Only manager 1 with 290 remains in the sample.

hints: Consider which groups from exercise 02 should remain.
Add HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 after GROUP BY managerId.
lessons.solution:
SELECT managerId, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
FROM Employee
WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY managerId
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

lessons.title: Show each employee's manager name
rules: Return employee_name and manager_name for employees who have managers.
Output columns · employee_name, manager_name
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Employees and managers are both in Employee. Alias the same table as e and m to read it in two roles.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT e.id AS employee_id, m.id AS manager_id
FROM Employee AS e
JOIN Employee AS m ON e.managerId = m.id
WHERE e.id = 9;
conceptExample.explanation: Ivo (id 9) has managerId 3. Joining to Cleo's manager-side row with id 3 returns 9 and 3.

hints: Which row's id matches the employee's managerId?
Join with FROM Employee AS e JOIN Employee AS m ON e.managerId = m.id.

lessons.title: Find manager names using WITH
rules: Return manager names and counts for managers with at least five direct reports. Aggregate first, then join to Employee.
Output columns · name, direct_reports
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: manager_counts is a name you choose for the intermediate result. The SELECT inside parentheses creates the aggregate result, which the outer SELECT reads.

conceptExample.explanation: Read the parentheses first: high_salary is an intermediate result with name and salary. The outer SELECT chooses only name. This chosen CTE name is valid only within the statement.

hints: Place the manager IDs and counts from exercise 03 inside WITH.
In the outer query, join Employee.id to manager_counts.managerId.
lessons.solution:
WITH manager_counts AS (
  SELECT managerId, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
  FROM Employee
  WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY managerId
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
)
SELECT e.name, c.direct_reports
FROM Employee AS e
JOIN manager_counts AS c ON e.id = c.managerId;
lessons.starter:
WITH manager_counts AS (
  -- Insert the aggregate query from exercise 03 here.
)
-- Return names and counts in the outer SELECT.

lessons.title: Put the same aggregation inside FROM
rules: Produce the same result as exercise 05 using a subquery. Return manager names and direct-report counts.
Output columns · name, direct_reports
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: A multirow subquery can act as a table in FROM or JOIN. An alias after the parentheses makes its columns easy to reference.

conceptExample.explanation: This matches the previous WITH example. Here, the intermediate result is inside FROM parentheses and immediately aliased as h.

hints: Run the manager aggregation independently before moving it inside parentheses.
Use JOIN (aggregate SELECT) AS c ON e.id = c.managerId.
lessons.solution:
SELECT e.name, c.direct_reports
FROM Employee AS e
JOIN (
  SELECT managerId, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
  FROM Employee
  WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY managerId
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
) AS c ON e.id = c.managerId;

lessons.title: Employees earning more than average
rules: Return names and salaries for employees earning more than the overall average salary.
Output columns · name, salary
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: A subquery used with > in WHERE returns one comparison value.

conceptExample.explanation: The inner MAX returns one value, 120, in the sample. The outer WHERE compares each employee's salary with it and keeps Ada.

hints: First run a SELECT returning just the average salary.
Connect them with WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employee).

lessons.title: Highest-grossing artists by genre
rules: Return artist name, genre, and concert revenue for artists with the highest concert revenue in their genre. Include all ties.
Output columns · artist_name, genre, concert_revenue
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: A correlated subquery can read the outer row. If the outer genre is Pop, the inner query finds the maximum for Pop.

conceptExample.explanation: The inner WHERE reads the outer genre and ID. EXISTS is true if another row has the same genre and a different ID.

hints: Alias the concert table as c outside and peer inside.
Restrict the inner SELECT with peer.genre = c.genre, then calculate MAX.
lessons.solution:
SELECT c.artist_name, c.genre, c.concert_revenue
FROM concerts AS c
WHERE c.concert_revenue = (
  SELECT MAX(peer.concert_revenue)
  FROM concerts AS peer
  WHERE peer.genre = c.genre
);

lessons.title: Find direct and indirect reports
rules: Return names and depth for all employees below a top-level manager (managerId is NULL). Direct reports have depth 1, their reports depth 2. Exclude top-level managers.
Output columns · name, depth
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: A recursive CTE selects starting rows, then joins to newly found rows to discover the next level.

conceptExample.explanation: SELECT 1 is the starting point. It generates 2 from 1, then 3 from 2, and stops at n < 3. For an employee hierarchy, replace numeric progression with a JOIN following reporting relationships.

hints: Start with top-level managers at depth 0.
Below UNION ALL, join Employee.managerId to the CTE's id and add 1 to depth.
lessons.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth
  FROM Employee
  WHERE managerId IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, r.depth + 1
  FROM Employee AS e
  JOIN reports AS r ON e.managerId = r.id
)
SELECT name, depth
FROM reports
WHERE depth > 0;

lessons.title: Add shop totals to every sale
rules: Return sale_id, shop, amount, and the shop's overall shop_total for every sale.
Output columns · sale_id, shop, amount, shop_total
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY shop) calculates shop totals while keeping the original sale rows.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT sale_id, shop, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY shop) AS sales_in_shop
FROM sales;
conceptExample.explanation: North has three sales in the sample, so each of those three rows gets 3. GROUP BY shop would collapse North to one row.

hints: There must be one output row per sale.
Add OVER (PARTITION BY shop) after SUM(amount).

lessons.title: Running sales totals by shop
rules: Return sale_id, shop, and running_total through each sale. Accumulate within each shop in sale_date, sale_id order.
Output columns · sale_id, shop, running_total
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Window ORDER BY defines calculation order. ROWS specifies the range of rows in that order.

conceptExample.explanation: Reading sales of 40 and 25 in order gives running totals of 40 and 65. Add PARTITION BY shop to restart for each shop.

hints: Use sale_id to order multiple sales on the same date.
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW spans the first row through the current row.

lessons.title: Compare rankings with ties
rules: Rank artists by revenue descending within each genre. Return artist_name, genre, revenue_rank from RANK, dense_rank from DENSE_RANK, and row_num from ROW_NUMBER. Break row_num ties by artist_id ascending.
Output columns · artist_name, genre, revenue_rank, dense_rank, row_num
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: For revenues 300,300,100, RANK gives 1,1,3 and DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2. ROW_NUMBER assigns a separate number to each row.

conceptExample.sql:
WITH scores(score) AS (VALUES (90), (90), (70))
SELECT score,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank_no,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS dense_no
FROM scores;
conceptExample.explanation: Two scores of 90 tie for first. A score of 70 is third with RANK and second with DENSE_RANK. Add a unique ID to ROW_NUMBER's ordering to make ties deterministic.

hints: Partition all three windows by genre.
Use only revenue in RANK and DENSE_RANK ordering to preserve ties. Also include artist_id for ROW_NUMBER.
lessons.solution:
SELECT artist_name, genre,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY genre ORDER BY concert_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY genre ORDER BY concert_revenue DESC) AS dense_rank,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY genre ORDER BY concert_revenue DESC, artist_id) AS row_num
FROM concerts;

lessons.title: Highest revenue per member in each genre
rules: Find artists with the highest revenue per member in each genre. Include all ties. Rank before rounding, then round only the final output to two decimal places.
Output columns · artist_name, genre, revenue_per_member
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Narrow the result in stages: row-level metric → genre-level ranking → select first place.

conceptExample.explanation: The inner SELECT numbers IDs within each genre. The outer WHERE selects number 1, giving the smallest-ID artist per genre.

hints: Use 1.0 * concert_revenue / number_of_members in SQLite for a fractional result.
Calculate RANK in a CTE, then select rank 1 in the outer WHERE.
lessons.solution:
WITH scored AS (
  SELECT artist_name, genre,
         1.0 * concert_revenue / number_of_members AS per_member
  FROM concerts
), ranked AS (
  SELECT artist_name, genre, per_member,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY genre ORDER BY per_member DESC) AS position
  FROM scored
)
SELECT artist_name, genre, ROUND(per_member, 2) AS revenue_per_member
FROM ranked
WHERE position = 1;

lessons.title: View previous and next sale amounts
rules: Return sale_id, previous_amount, and next_amount within the same shop. Order by sale_date, sale_id within each shop.
Output columns · sale_id, previous_amount, next_amount
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: LAG reads the previous row in an ordered window; LEAD reads the next. Missing rows default to NULL.

conceptExample.explanation: The first sale has no previous row, so it returns NULL. The second sale's previous_amount is 40. LEAD reads the following row in the same order.

hints: Keep sale rows while retrieving neighbouring amount values.
Use OVER (PARTITION BY shop ORDER BY sale_date, sale_id) for both functions.
lessons.solution:
SELECT sale_id,
       LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY shop ORDER BY sale_date, sale_id) AS previous_amount,
       LEAD(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY shop ORDER BY sale_date, sale_id) AS next_amount
FROM sales;

lessons.title: Combine customer lists from two months
rules: Return every customer ID appearing in January or February exactly once.
Output columns · customer_id
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: UNION combines results and removes duplicates. UNION ALL preserves duplicate rows.

conceptExample.explanation: UNION ALL returns the value 1 twice as two rows. UNION keeps one. Both SELECT statements need the same number of columns.

hints: Both SELECT statements return one column.
Place UNION between the SELECT statements.

lessons.title: Find customers appearing only in January
rules: Return each customer ID that appears in January but not February, once.
Output columns · customer_id
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: INTERSECT returns rows in both results; EXCEPT returns rows only in the left result.

conceptExample.explanation: In the sample, 2 and 3 remain because they appear in both months. Replacing INTERSECT with EXCEPT subtracts right-side IDs from the left list.

hints: Which month should be subtracted from which?
Put SELECT customer_id FROM january before EXCEPT.

lessons.title: Which condition belongs where?
rules: Calculate shop totals using online sales only. Keep shops whose online total is at least 40. Order by total descending, then shop name ascending.
Output columns · shop, online_total
lessons.concept: Think logically: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY to place each condition correctly.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT shop, COUNT(*) AS sale_count
FROM sales
WHERE amount >= 30
GROUP BY shop
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY sale_count DESC;
conceptExample.explanation: First select sales of at least 30, then count by shop and keep shops with at least two sales. The final ORDER BY sorts the remaining results.

hints: Separate conditions evaluable on a single sale from conditions evaluated per shop.
Select rows with WHERE channel and groups with HAVING SUM(amount).
lessons.solution:
SELECT shop, SUM(amount) AS online_total
FROM sales
WHERE channel = 'online'
GROUP BY shop
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 40
ORDER BY online_total DESC, shop;

lessons.title: Online and store revenue in two columns
rules: Return one row per shop with online_sales and store_sales as separate columns. Use 0 when a channel has no sales.
Output columns · shop, online_sales, store_sales
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Conditional aggregation splits an aggregate by column values. CASE determines which amounts contribute.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT shop,
       SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'online' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS online_orders
FROM sales
GROUP BY shop;
conceptExample.explanation: CASE produces 1 for each online sale; SUM counts online sales per shop. Replacing THEN 1 with THEN amount changes the count to revenue.

hints: Use GROUP BY shop for one row per shop.
Apply SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'online' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) to both channels.
lessons.solution:
SELECT shop,
       SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'online' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS online_sales,
       SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'store' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS store_sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY shop;

lessons.title: Turn channel revenue columns back into rows
rules: Return online and store revenue as separate rows per shop. Set channel to online or store and include zero revenue.
Output columns · shop, channel, amount
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Build a SELECT with the same shape for each column, then stack with UNION ALL to turn column values into rows.

conceptExample.sql:
WITH one_shop(shop, online_sales, store_sales) AS (VALUES ('North', 55, 25))
SELECT shop, 'online' AS channel, online_sales AS amount FROM one_shop
UNION ALL
SELECT shop, 'store' AS channel, store_sales AS amount FROM one_shop;
conceptExample.explanation: One North row becomes North, online, 55 and North, store, 25. Each SELECT reads one revenue column and labels its channel.

hints: Each SELECT must produce shop, channel, and amount.
The first SELECT uses 'online' AS channel and online_sales AS amount. Connect the results with UNION ALL.

lessons.title: Clean names and extract email domains
rules: Find customers whose trimmed name ends with son, ignoring case. Return customer_id, trimmed clean_name, and lowercase email_domain. Each email contains one @.
Output columns · customer_id, clean_name, email_domain
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: TRIM removes surrounding spaces and LOWER converts to lowercase. Combine INSTR and SUBSTR to extract text after a delimiter.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT LOWER(TRIM('  ADA Kim  ')) AS clean_name,
       SUBSTR('ada@example.com', INSTR('ada@example.com', '@') + 1) AS domain;
conceptExample.explanation: The first column is ada kim. INSTR locates @; +1 points to the next character, so SUBSTR extracts example.com.

hints: Try LIKE '%son' on LOWER(TRIM(customer_name)).
INSTR(email, '@') gives the @ position. Use SUBSTR from the next character.
lessons.solution:
SELECT customer_id, TRIM(customer_name) AS clean_name,
       LOWER(SUBSTR(email, INSTR(email, '@') + 1)) AS email_domain
FROM customers
WHERE LOWER(TRIM(customer_name)) LIKE '%son';

lessons.title: Count products reordered in February
rules: Return product names and reorders for February 2026. Count only order items with reordered=1 and aggregate by product ID.
Output columns · product_name, reorders
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Define what each output row represents to know what to count after a JOIN. Here, count repeat-purchase rows per product.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, i.product_id
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id
WHERE o.order_id = 2;
conceptExample.explanation: Order 2 has two products in the sample, so the join returns two rows. COUNT(*) after this JOIN counts order items, not orders.

hints: You need dates from orders and reordered from order_items. product_name is in products.
Filter dates from February 1 inclusive to March 1 exclusive. Each order item is one counted record.
lessons.solution:
SELECT p.product_name, COUNT(*) AS reorders
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-02-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-03-01'
  AND i.reordered = 1
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name;

lessons.title: Products with more reorders than in January
rules: Find products with fewer than two reorders in January 2026 and at least two in February. Return product names and counts for both months. Months with no reorders count as 0.
Output columns · product_name, january_reorders, february_reorders
Rows may appear in any order.
lessons.concept: Readable queries give intermediate results clear roles. Verify monthly aggregates first, then attach product names and apply change conditions outside.

conceptExample.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN order_date >= '2026-02-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS feb_orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-03-01'
GROUP BY customer_id;
conceptExample.explanation: First select January–February orders. Adding 1 for February and 0 for January gives February orders per customer. In this exercise, group by product instead.

hints: Join orders and order_items and select only January–February reorder rows.
Create two SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) columns per product in a monthly CTE, then compare them in the outer WHERE.
lessons.solution:
WITH monthly_reorders AS (
  SELECT i.product_id,
         SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_date < '2026-02-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS january_reorders,
         SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_date >= '2026-02-01' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS february_reorders
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-03-01'
    AND i.reordered = 1
  GROUP BY i.product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name, m.january_reorders, m.february_reorders
FROM monthly_reorders AS m
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = m.product_id
WHERE m.january_reorders < 2 AND m.february_reorders >= 2;
